# 1. Assessment Rubrics

---

## Assessment 1: Central Dogma Mutation Model

### Teacher-Facing Analytic Rubric

| Criterion (NGSS Alignment) | 4 — Exceeds | 3 — Meets | 2 — Approaching | 1 — Beginning | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Model accuracy** (SEP: Developing & Using Models; HS-LS1-1) | All base pairing, codons, and amino acids are correct; model clearly distinguishes replication, transcription, and translation with accurate labels and directionality (5'→3') | All base pairing and codon reading correct; all three processes shown and labeled; minor omission (e.g., directionality missing) | 1–2 base-pairing or codon-reading errors OR one process is missing or mislabeled | Multiple errors in base pairing or codon reading; processes are confused or absent | /4 |
| **Mutation analysis** (HS-LS3-2) | Correctly introduces the assigned mutation, traces its effect through transcription and translation, and accurately classifies it (silent, missense, nonsense, or frameshift) with explanation of why | Correctly introduces mutation and traces its effect; classification is stated but explanation is thin | Mutation is introduced but its effect on the protein is only partially or incorrectly traced | Mutation is not introduced or its downstream effect is not addressed | /4 |
| **Claim-Evidence-Reasoning paragraph** (SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence) | Claim directly addresses phenotype change; evidence cites specific sequence positions and amino acid changes; reasoning explicitly connects protein structure/function to phenotype | Claim addresses phenotype; evidence references sequence; reasoning connects protein to phenotype but lacks specificity | Claim is present but vague; evidence or reasoning is missing or disconnected | No clear claim, or evidence and reasoning are both absent | /4 |
| **Heritability statement** (HS-LS3-3) | Correctly states whether the mutation is heritable, distinguishes somatic vs. germline, and explains why | Correctly states heritability with brief justification | Statement is present but justification is missing or inaccurate | Not addressed | /4 |
| **Model communication & neatness** (SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, Communicating Information) | Model is easy to read, uses a clear key/legend, and could be understood without verbal explanation | Model is legible and mostly self-explanatory; minor clarity issues | Model requires significant verbal explanation to interpret | Model is disorganized or illegible | /4 |

**Total: /20**

### Student Checklist — Assessment 1

> **Central Dogma Mutation Model: "I Can" Checklist**
>
> Use this before you submit. Check each box honestly.
>
> **My model shows:**
> - [ ] The original DNA strand and its complementary strand with correct base pairing (A-T, C-G)
> - [ ] The mRNA strand transcribed from the template strand with correct base pairing (A-U, C-G)
> - [ ] The amino acid sequence translated from the mRNA using the codon chart
> - [ ] Clear labels for replication, transcription, and translation
> - [ ] A key or legend so someone else can read it without my help
>
> **My mutation analysis shows:**
> - [ ] The specific mutation I introduced (type and location)
> - [ ] The new mRNA and new amino acid sequence after the mutation
> - [ ] The name of the mutation effect (silent, missense, nonsense, or frameshift)
>
> **My CER paragraph includes:**
> - [ ] A claim that says whether the mutation changes the phenotype
> - [ ] Evidence that points to the exact sequence and amino acid change
> - [ ] Reasoning that explains how the changed protein affects the organism
>
> **My heritability sentence:**
> - [ ] States whether this mutation could be passed to offspring
> - [ ] Explains why (somatic vs. germline)

---

## Assessment 2: Family Inheritance Investigation

### Teacher-Facing Analytic Rubric

| Criterion (NGSS Alignment) | 4 — Exceeds | 3 — Meets | 2 — Approaching | 1 — Beginning | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Inheritance pattern identification** (HS-LS3-1) | Correctly identifies pattern (AD, AR, or X-linked); justification cites at least two specific pedigree relationships (e.g., "Two unaffected parents have an affected child, which rules out dominant") | Correct pattern with one piece of pedigree evidence | Correct pattern but no evidence, or incorrect pattern with reasonable evidence | Pattern is incorrect and unjustified | /4 |
| **Genotype assignment** (HS-LS3-1) | All assigned genotypes are correct and consistent with the stated pattern; uncertainties are noted (e.g., "Bb or BB — cannot determine without more data") | All assigned genotypes correct; uncertainties not addressed | 1–2 genotype errors or inconsistency with stated pattern | Most genotypes missing or incorrect | /4 |
| **Probability calculation** (SEP: Using Mathematics; HS-LS3-3) | Punnett square is correct; probability is stated as fraction, decimal, and/or percent; interpretation sentence is accurate | Punnett square correct; probability stated in one form; interpretation present | Punnett square has an error that leads to an incorrect probability, but method is sound | Punnett square missing or fundamentally flawed | /4 |
| **Chi-square analysis** (SEP: Analyzing & Interpreting Data; HS-LS3-3) | Expected values, χ² calculation, and degrees of freedom are all correct; student correctly compares to critical value and states whether to reject or fail to reject the null; explains what variation means | Calculation correct; comparison to critical value correct; interpretation is present but brief | Calculation has a minor arithmetic error or interpretation is missing | Chi-square not attempted or fundamentally incorrect | /4 |
| **Family letter communication** (SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, Communicating Information) | Accurate science translated into accessible language; tone is empathetic; probability is explained without jargon; limitations of prediction are noted | Accurate and accessible; minor jargon or tone issues | Some inaccuracies or largely inaccessible language | Not attempted or scientifically inaccurate | /4 |

**Total: /20**

### Student Checklist — Assessment 2

> **Family Inheritance Investigation: "I Can" Checklist**
>
> - [ ] I identified the inheritance pattern and explained why, using specific people in the pedigree as evidence
> - [ ] I assigned genotypes to every individual the teacher specified
> - [ ] I noted any genotypes I cannot determine for certain and explained why
> - [ ] I drew a correct Punnett square for the requested cross
> - [ ] I stated the probability of the future child being affected (fraction, percent, or both)
> - [ ] I calculated expected offspring numbers from the class simulation data
> - [ ] I completed a chi-square table (observed, expected, (O−E)²/E for each category)
> - [ ] I compared my χ² value to the critical value and stated whether the data fit the model
> - [ ] I wrote a family letter that explains the results in plain, respectful language
> - [ ] My letter mentions that predictions are probabilities, not certainties

---

## Assessment 3: Gene Editing Policy Brief

### Teacher-Facing Analytic Rubric

| Criterion (NGSS Alignment) | 4 — Exceeds | 3 — Meets | 2 — Approaching | 1 — Beginning | Pts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Scientific accuracy** (HS-LS3-2; HS-LS1-1) | Mechanism of the technology (e.g., how CRISPR creates a double-strand break and repair introduces an edit) is explained accurately and connected to prior unit content (mutation types, gene expression) | Mechanism is mostly accurate with a clear connection to mutation or gene expression concepts | Mechanism is oversimplified or contains a minor scientific error | Mechanism is absent or contains major errors | /4 |
| **Use of evidence** (SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence) | Cites at least two provided sources; includes at least one quantitative data point (e.g., efficacy rate, off-target frequency); data are interpreted, not just quoted | Two sources cited; one quantitative data point included; interpretation is present but surface-level | One source cited or no quantitative data; evidence is present but weak | No evidence from sources | /4 |
| **Unintended consequences** (CCC: Cause & Effect; HS-LS3-2) | Identifies at least one unintended consequence and explicitly connects it to genetic concepts (e.g., off-target edits creating new mutations, reducing allele diversity in a population) | Identifies an unintended consequence with a general connection to genetics | Mentions a risk but does not connect it to genetics | Not addressed | /4 |
| **Counterargument & rebuttal** (SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence) | Presents a substantive counterargument from a named stakeholder perspective; rebuttal uses evidence and reasoning | Counterargument and rebuttal present but one is underdeveloped | Only a counterargument or only a rebuttal, not both | Neither present | /4 |
| **Clarity, structure, & audience awareness** (SEP: Obtaining, Evaluating, Communicating Information; ETS1.B) | Brief follows a logical structure (claim → evidence → consequences → counterargument → conclusion); language is appropriate for a policy audience; within page limit | Structure is clear; minor organizational or tone issues | Structure is unclear or significantly over/under length | Disorganized; difficult to follow | /4 |

**Total: /20**

### Student Checklist — Assessment 3

> **Gene Editing Policy Brief: "I Can" Checklist**
>
> - [ ] I explained how the technology works at the DNA level, using vocabulary from this unit (mutation type, gene expression, protein function)
> - [ ] I stated a clear policy claim (e.g., "CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease should be approved for clinical use with the following safeguards…")
> - [ ] I cited at least two sources from the provided packet
> - [ ] I included at least one piece of quantitative data and explained what it means
> - [ ] I described at least one unintended consequence and connected it to genetics
> - [ ] I included a counterargument from a different stakeholder's point of view
> - [ ] I responded to the counterargument with evidence or reasoning
> - [ ] My brief is 1–2 pages and organized so a reader can follow my argument
> - [ ] I proofread for scientific accuracy and clarity

---

# 2. Week 1 Materials & Prep: Mutation Model

## Physical Option
- **Colored pop beads or pipe cleaners** (4 colors = 4 bases); ~30 per student pair
- **Printed codon chart** (1 per student)
- **Card-stock nucleotide cutouts** (alternative to beads; template takes ~20 min to prep; students cut)
- **Mutation task cards** (set of 6, each specifying a mutation type and position; ~15 min to create)

**Estimated prep:** 45–60 min first time; 15 min in subsequent years

## Digital Option
- **Google Slides template** with drag-and-drop nucleotide shapes (create once, share via LMS; ~30 min to build)
- **Or use the free "DNA Protein Synthesis" PhET simulation** — no prep beyond writing a guided handout (~20 min)

## Both Options Need
- Short DNA sequence handout (8–12 codons; include start and stop); 10 min to write
- CER paragraph scaffold/frame (downloadable or one-page handout); 10 min
- Printed student checklist (above)

**Total first-time prep:** ~1.5 hrs physical, ~1 hr digital

# Week 1 Lesson Plans

---

## Day 1: Intro to DNA Structure & the Central Dogma (50 min)

### Learning Objectives (HS-LS1-1; SEP: Developing & Using Models)
- Students will describe the structure of DNA (nucleotide components, base pairing, antiparallel strands) and explain why complementary base pairing is essential for replication.
- Students will trace the flow of genetic information from DNA → mRNA → protein and explain the role of each step in one sentence.

---

### Lesson Sequence

| Time | Phase | What Happens |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:06 | **Opener: "What makes a copy reliable?"** | Show two images side by side: a photocopy of a sentence that is perfect and one that has obvious errors. Ask: *"What would a cell need to copy a 3-billion-letter instruction manual with almost no mistakes?"* Students write a 2-sentence prediction in their notebooks. Cold-call 2–3 students to share. Bridge to DNA structure: "Let's look at the built-in feature that makes high-fidelity copying possible." |
| 0:06–0:16 | **Direct instruction: DNA structure** | Mini-lecture/slides (keep to ~10 min). Cover: nucleotide (sugar, phosphate, base), A-T / C-G pairing with hydrogen bonds, antiparallel orientation, double helix. Use a labeled diagram students annotate in guided notes. |
| 0:16–0:20 | **Quick check** | Think-pair-share: *"If one strand reads 5'-ATCGGA-3', what does the complementary strand read? Include directionality."* Teacher circulates and listens; correct common errors (forgetting to flip directionality). |
| 0:20–0:22 | **Transition & framing** | "Structure enables function. Now let's see the three jobs that depend on base pairing: replication, transcription, translation." Hand out the Central Dogma Flowchart activity sheet. |
| 0:22–0:47 | **Student activity: Central Dogma Flowchart Build (25 min)** | Students work in pairs. Each pair receives an envelope with **12 pre-printed sentence strips** (4 per process: replication, transcription, translation) that describe key events (e.g., "RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and reads the template strand 3'→5'"). Strips are **color-coded by process** but arrive shuffled. **Task:** (1) Sort strips into three columns. (2) Arrange each column in correct order. (3) Glue onto a tri-fold flowchart and draw arrows showing information flow. (4) Add a one-sentence summary under each column: *"The purpose of this step is…"* Teacher circulates with a key; stamps or initials correct flowcharts. |
| 0:47–0:50 | **Exit ticket (3 min)** | On an index card: *"A mutation changes a single base in a gene. Name the first process in which that change would appear and explain why it matters for the protein."* Collect at the door. |

---

### Differentiation

| Need | Strategy |
|---|---|
| **Scaffolded support** | Provide sentence strips pre-sorted by color with column headers already on the flowchart; include a word bank for summary sentences. |
| **On-level** | Activity as described above. |
| **Extension** | Remove color coding from strips; add two distractor strips (e.g., a statement about cell division that does not belong) students must identify and discard with a written reason. |
| **ELL / reading support** | Pair with a strong reader; sentence strips include a bolded key vocabulary word with a parenthetical definition; guided notes have diagrams with blank labels rather than blank sentences. |

---
---

## Day 2: Mutation Model Build & Walkthrough (90 min lab)

### Learning Objectives (HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-2; SEP: Developing & Using Models)
- Students will model replication, transcription, and translation using a provided DNA sequence and demonstrate correct base pairing and codon reading.
- Students will introduce an assigned mutation, trace its effect through the central dogma, and classify the result (silent, missense, nonsense, or frameshift).

### Materials (per pair)
- Pop beads or pipe-cleaner segments in 4 colors (or digital Slides template)
- Printed codon chart
- 8-codon DNA sequence handout (includes start codon context)
- One mutation task card (drawn at random)
- CER paragraph scaffold
- Student checklist (from rubric packet)

---

### Step-by-Step Timing

| Time | Phase | Teacher Prompts / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | **Warm-up** | Display yesterday's exit-ticket results (anonymized). Show one strong answer and one common misconception. Ask: *"What would we need to add to make the second answer stronger?"* |
| 0:05–0:12 | **Demo & expectations (7 min)** | Model the first 2 codons of the sequence under a document camera (physical) or screen-share (digital). Talk aloud: *"I read the template strand 3'→5' so my mRNA is built 5'→3'… my first codon is AUG, which codes for methionine — that's my start."* Show how to lay out / snap pieces. State lab norms: voices at conversation level, all materials stay on the tray, both partners build (one strand each). |
| 0:12–0:14 | **Distribute materials & task cards** | Each pair draws one mutation task card at random (see list below). Read it silently, then confirm understanding with partner. Teacher circulates to verify. |
| 0:14–0:40 | **Build Phase 1: Wild-type model (26 min)** | Partners build the full normal sequence through replication, transcription, and translation. **Circulate and use checkpoint prompts:** *"Point to where transcription is happening. Which strand is the template? Why did you choose that amino acid?"* Stamp/initial when the wild-type model is verified correct. **No pair moves to Phase 2 without a stamp.** |
| 0:40–0:45 | **Midpoint pause (5 min)** | Whole-class: call on 2–3 pairs to share one thing that surprised them or one mistake they caught. Briefly re-teach any widespread error (common: using the coding strand instead of template for mRNA). |
| 0:45–1:05 | **Build Phase 2: Mutant model (20 min)** | Pairs duplicate their model, introduce the assigned mutation at the specified position, and trace the new mRNA and amino acid sequence. **Circulate and prompt:** *"How many amino acids changed? Why did everything after this point shift? What would happen to the protein's shape?"* |
| 1:05–1:20 | **CER writing (15 min)** | Pairs write their claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph using the scaffold. Each student writes their own copy. **Prompt on board:** *"Claim: State whether your mutation changes the phenotype. Evidence: Cite the exact codon and amino acid change. Reasoning: Explain how the protein is affected and why that matters for the organism."* |
| 1:20–1:27 | **Gallery walk (7 min)** | Pairs place models and CER paragraphs on desks. Students walk, read two other pairs' work, and leave one sticky-note comment: *"One thing your model helped me understand…"* or *"One question I still have about your mutation…"* |
| 1:27–1:30 | **Cleanup & close (3 min)** | Materials returned to trays. Teacher collects CER paragraphs. Closing prompt (verbal, cold-call): *"Which type of mutation do you think is most dangerous to an organism, and why?"* Preview Day 3. |

---

### Safety & Management Tips
- **No loose beads on the floor** — provide trays or paper plates to contain pieces.
- **Digital option** eliminates small-parts management; ideal for classes with limited physical supplies or mobility considerations.
- **Assign roles** (Strand Builder A / Strand Builder B) so both students are hands-on.
- **Early finishers:** answer the extension question on the task card (see below) or begin revising their flowchart from Day 1 to include mutation.

---

### Informal Lab Assessment Rubric (Teacher Use During Circulating)

| Criterion | ✓+ (Strong) | ✓ (Adequate) | ✓− (Needs support) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Base pairing accuracy** | No errors in DNA or mRNA | 1 minor error, self-corrected when prompted | Multiple errors; needed direct re-teaching |
| **Codon reading** | Correct reading frame; amino acids match codon chart | 1 amino acid error | Reading frame incorrect or codon chart not used |
| **Mutation application** | Mutation introduced at correct position; downstream effects accurately traced | Mutation introduced correctly; downstream trace has a minor error | Mutation not introduced correctly or effects not traced |
| **CER quality** | Claim, evidence, and reasoning all present and logically connected | One element is weak or vague | Two or more elements missing |
| **Collaboration** | Both partners building, discussing, and writing | One partner dominant but both engaged when prompted | One partner disengaged; intervention needed |

*Record as ✓+, ✓, or ✓− per pair on a class roster. Use ✓− marks to identify pairs needing follow-up before the summative model assessment.*

---

## Mutation Task Cards (Print, Cut, and Shuffle — One per Pair)

1. **Point mutation — Silent:** Change the third nucleotide of codon 4 from C to A. Determine whether the amino acid changes. *Extension: Why are silent mutations most common at the third position of a codon?*

2. **Point mutation — Missense:** Change the first nucleotide of codon 5 from A to G. Identify the new amino acid and predict whether the protein's function might change. *Extension: Under what circumstances could a missense mutation be beneficial?*

3. **Point mutation — Nonsense:** Change the second nucleotide of codon 6 from A to G so that the codon becomes UAG. Describe what happens to translation. *Extension: How might a cell's quality-control systems respond to a shortened protein?*

4. **Insertion (frameshift):** Insert a T between the first and second nucleotides of codon 3. Retranslate from that point forward and describe what happens to every downstream amino acid. *Extension: Would inserting three nucleotides cause the same kind of damage? Why or why not?*

5. **Deletion (frameshift):** Delete the second nucleotide of codon 4. Retranslate from that point forward and compare the new amino acid chain to the original. *Extension: If this gene encodes an enzyme, predict the effect on the reaction the enzyme catalyzes.*

6. **Deletion — Single amino acid loss (in-frame):** Delete all three nucleotides of codon 7. Determine how many amino acids are lost and whether the reading frame is preserved. *Extension: Why might losing one amino acid be less harmful than a frameshift, and when might it still be devastating?*

# Day 3: Summative Assessment — Central Dogma Mutation Model (50 min)

### Learning Objectives (HS-LS1-1, HS-LS3-2; SEP: Developing & Using Models, Engaging in Argument from Evidence)
- Students will independently model replication, transcription, and translation from a novel DNA sequence, introduce an assigned mutation, and construct a written CER argument connecting the mutation to a phenotype change.

---

### Important Distinctions from Day 2
- **New sequence** (not the practice sequence from Day 2; same length — 8 codons)
- **Individual work** (not pairs)
- **New mutation task card** (each student draws one at random; same 6 types, different codon positions than Day 2)

---

### Timed Sequence

| Time | Task | Student Produces |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:03 | Read instructions, receive sequence handout, draw mutation card, ask clarifying questions | — |
| 0:03–0:20 | **Wild-type model build** (physical or digital, same format practiced Day 2) | Annotated model showing DNA → mRNA → amino acid chain with labels for each process |
| 0:20–0:35 | **Mutation model build** — introduce assigned mutation, re-translate from mutation point forward | Side-by-side mutant model; mutation type and location labeled; changed amino acids highlighted or circled |
| 0:35–0:47 | **Written components** | (1) CER paragraph: claim about phenotype effect, sequence evidence, protein-function reasoning. (2) One-sentence heritability statement (somatic vs. germline). |
| 0:47–0:50 | Self-check against printed student checklist, staple checklist to model, submit | Completed packet: model + CER + checklist |

**Deliverable summary:** One packet per student containing the annotated wild-type model, the annotated mutant model, the CER paragraph, the heritability sentence, and the self-checked student checklist.

---

### Accommodations

| Need | Accommodation |
|---|---|
| **IEP / 504 — extended time** | Student completes wild-type model in class, finishes mutation + CER in resource period or designated extended-time room; provide a sealable bag for physical model pieces |
| **IEP / 504 — reduced written output** | Accept a bulleted CER instead of a full paragraph; require the same three elements (claim, evidence, reasoning) |
| **ELL** | Provide a bilingual codon chart if available; allow labeled diagrams in place of full sentences for the model annotations; CER sentence starters printed on the scaffold ("My claim is… My evidence is… This matters because…") |
| **Physical / motor** | Default to digital Slides template; allow voice-typed CER paragraph |
| **Early finishers** | Answer the extension question on their task card in writing on the back of the CER sheet |

---

### Realistic Scoring Plan (~25 students)

| Strategy | Detail |
|---|---|
| **First-pass sort (same day, ~20 min)** | Stack models into three piles while scanning: (1) clearly meets — no obvious base-pairing or reading-frame errors, CER complete; (2) borderline — minor errors or thin reasoning; (3) needs follow-up — major errors or missing components. This immediately identifies students who need re-teaching before Week 2. |
| **Detailed scoring (next planning period or evening, ~40 min)** | Score only the borderline pile criterion by criterion using the analytic rubric. For the "clearly meets" pile, confirm the score with a quick rubric check and record. For the "needs follow-up" pile, score fully and write one specific feedback comment per student. |
| **Student self-check as first filter** | Because students submit the checklist attached, glance at unchecked boxes first — they tell you exactly where the student knew they were incomplete, saving diagnostic time. |
| **Return timeline** | Scores and feedback returned by Day 5 (start of Week 2) so students see results before the inheritance unit begins. |

---

### Teacher Set-Up & Grading Checklist (Printable)

> **Day 3 — Before Class**
> - [ ] Print novel 8-codon DNA sequence handout (1 per student)
> - [ ] Print or adjust mutation task cards with new codon positions (6 types; enough copies so each student draws one at random)
> - [ ] Print student checklists (1 per student)
> - [ ] Print CER scaffold with sentence starters (for ELL and IEP students; extras available for anyone)
> - [ ] Set out materials trays (physical) or confirm Slides template is shared and editable (digital)
> - [ ] Print codon charts (1 per student; bilingual copies flagged for ELL students)
> - [ ] Prepare sealable bags for extended-time students' physical models
> - [ ] Post timer or have phone/projector timer ready
>
> **During Class**
> - [ ] Read instructions aloud; clarify that this is individual work
> - [ ] Start visible timer at 0:03
> - [ ] Circulate silently — answer clarifying questions about procedure only, not content
> - [ ] Give 5-minute warning at 0:42
> - [ ] Remind students to self-check and staple checklist before submitting
> - [ ] Collect extended-time students' partial work and issue bags/deadline passes
>
> **After Class**
> - [ ] First-pass sort into three piles (meets / borderline / follow-up): aim for same day
> - [ ] Detailed rubric scoring by end of Day 4
> - [ ] Record scores in gradebook
> - [ ] Write one targeted feedback comment per "follow-up" student
> - [ ] Return scored assessments on Day 5
> - [ ] Note patterns (most common error type) to address in a 3-minute warm-up on Day 5

# Week 2 Lesson Plans

---

## Day 4: Intro to Mendelian Crosses (50 min)

### Learning Objectives (HS-LS3-1; SEP: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking)
- Students will define allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, and recessive and use correct notation in genetic crosses.
- Students will construct Punnett squares for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and calculate predicted genotypic and phenotypic ratios.

---

### Lesson Sequence

| Time | Phase | What Happens |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:06 | **Opener: "Why don't families look like clones?"** | Display photos of a dog litter with varied coat colors (same two parents). Ask: *"These puppies have the same mom and dad. Why don't they all look the same? Write two possible explanations."* Cold-call 3 students. Bridge: *"Mendel figured this out with peas — and the tool he needed fits in a 2×2 box."* |
| 0:06–0:16 | **Direct instruction: Mendel's model** | Mini-lecture (~10 min). Cover: alleles as gene variants, dominant/recessive, homozygous/heterozygous, genotype vs. phenotype. Demonstrate one monohybrid cross (Bb × Bb) on the board, narrating every step: *"I put parent 1's alleles on top, parent 2's on the side, then combine — each box is one equally likely outcome."* Students copy into guided notes. |
| 0:16–0:18 | **Quick check** | Thumbs up / sideways / down: *"Could two brown-eyed parents have a blue-eyed child?"* Call on a sideways or down student to explain their thinking; correct in real time. |
| 0:18–0:45 | **Active practice: Punnett Square Ladder (27 min)** | Students work individually, moving through a scaffolded problem set printed on a single sheet. **Rung 1 (monohybrid, guided):** Bb × Bb — fill in a pre-drawn square, list genotypic and phenotypic ratios. Answer key printed upside-down at the bottom of the section so students self-check before moving on. **Rung 2 (monohybrid, independent):** Ff × ff — draw their own square, predict ratios, write one sentence: *"The chance of a homozygous recessive offspring is ___ because ___."* **Rung 3 (dihybrid, scaffolded):** BbFf × BbFf — a 4×4 grid is provided with gamete-determination steps walked through (*"List all possible gametes for BbFf: BF, Bf, bF, bf"*). Students fill in the grid and calculate the phenotypic ratio. **Rung 4 (extension):** *"A breeder wants to guarantee all offspring show the dominant phenotype for both traits. What parental genotypes are needed? Justify."* Teacher circulates with a roster checklist, initialing when students complete Rung 2 correctly (minimum expectation). |
| 0:45–0:47 | **Debrief** | Display completed dihybrid square. Ask: *"What ratio did you get? Does 9:3:3:1 remind you of any fractions? Why might real data not match perfectly?"* Bridge to chi-square on Day 5. |
| 0:47–0:50 | **Exit ticket** | *"A plant with genotype RrYy is crossed with rryy. How many phenotype categories will appear in the offspring, and what are their predicted ratios? Show your Punnett square."* Collect. |

---

### Differentiation

| Need | Strategy |
|---|---|
| **Scaffolded support** | Provide a laminated Punnett square template with labeled rows/columns; allow students to use letter tiles instead of writing. Students complete Rungs 1–2; Rung 3 is attempted with teacher support. |
| **On-level** | Activity as described; must reach Rung 3 independently. |
| **Extension** | Rung 4 required; additional prompt: *"Why does independent assortment break down when two genes are on the same chromosome?"* (preview of linkage if in your scope). |
| **ELL** | Vocabulary card with term, definition, and labeled diagram for each key word (allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive); pair with a fluent partner for Rung 3. |

---

### Common Misconceptions to Watch For

Students frequently believe that a 3:1 ratio means exactly 3 out of every 4 offspring will show the dominant phenotype, rather than understanding it as a probability that becomes visible only in large sample sizes. They also confuse the genotype of the offspring box with the probability of that outcome, thinking that filling in "Bb" in two boxes means the organism has two copies of Bb. Watch for students who set up dihybrid gametes incorrectly by pairing alleles from the same gene (BB, bb) instead of one allele from each gene (Bf, bF). Finally, many students assume dominant means "more common" or "better"; address this explicitly by naming a dominant trait that is rare (e.g., polydactyly).

---
---

## Day 5: Pedigree Analysis + Chi-Square Class Simulation (90 min lab)

### Learning Objectives (HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-3; SEP: Analyzing & Interpreting Data, Using Mathematics)
- Students will determine the most likely inheritance pattern from a three-generation pedigree and assign genotypes with evidence.
- Students will generate offspring data through a physical simulation, apply a chi-square test, and interpret whether the data support the predicted Mendelian ratio.
- Students will communicate inheritance results to a nonscientist audience in a short family letter.

### Materials (per pair)
- Printed pedigree handout (fictional family, autosomal recessive trait, 3 generations, 12–15 individuals)
- Two coins (one per parent allele; heads = dominant, tails = recessive)
- Class data recording sheet (projected Google Sheet or whiteboard table)
- Chi-square calculation template (pre-formatted table: Observed, Expected, O−E, (O−E)², (O−E)²/E)
- Chi-square critical value reference strip (df = 1, 2, 3; p = 0.05)
- Family letter scaffold (greeting, body paragraph prompts, closing)
- Student checklist from Assessment 2 rubric packet

---

### Step-by-Step Timing

| Time | Phase | Teacher Prompts / Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | **Warm-up** | Return scored exit tickets from Day 4. Display one common gamete error from dihybrid crosses (anonymized). Students correct it on whiteboards. |
| 0:05–0:12 | **Pedigree conventions mini-lesson (7 min)** | Projected slide: squares, circles, shading, horizontal lines (mating), vertical lines (offspring). Walk through one example pedigree for a dominant trait. Key prompt: *"What is the first question you should always ask when you see a pedigree?"* → *"Can two unaffected parents have an affected child?"* If yes → recessive. |
| 0:12–0:32 | **Pedigree analysis — independent work (20 min)** | Students receive the fictional pedigree. **Task 1:** Determine inheritance pattern and write a 2-sentence justification citing specific individuals by number (e.g., *"Individuals 4 and 5 are unaffected but have an affected child (Individual 9), which rules out dominant"*). **Task 2:** Assign genotypes to all individuals the handout specifies (starred); note any that cannot be determined with certainty and explain why. **Task 3:** Punnett square for a specified cross (e.g., Individuals 4 × 5); state probability of next child being affected. Teacher circulates; stamp genotype assignments when correct. **Prompt for stuck students:** *"Start with the affected individuals — what must their genotype be? Now work backward to the parents."* |
| 0:32–0:37 | **Transition to simulation** | *"You just predicted a ratio. But does nature follow the prediction perfectly? Let's find out."* Explain simulation: each pair flips two coins 40 times (one coin = one parent's allele contribution for the cross they just solved). Record offspring genotype each flip. |
| 0:37–0:57 | **Coin-flip simulation (20 min)** | Pairs flip and tally. One partner flips, one records. After 40 flips, pairs report totals to the class data table (projected). Teacher tallies class totals (aiming for ~400+ total flips across all pairs). **Management tips:** (1) Provide small cups for flipping to control noise and runaway coins. (2) Have pairs double-check each other's tallies before reporting. (3) If a pair finishes early, they begin calculating their own pair's chi-square while waiting for class data. |
| 0:57–1:02 | **Class data review (5 min)** | Display completed class data table. Ask: *"Do the observed numbers match the expected ratio exactly? Should they? Why not?"* Introduce chi-square: *"This test tells us whether the difference between observed and expected is small enough to be explained by chance."* |
| 1:02–1:17 | **Chi-square calculation (15 min)** | Students use the template to calculate χ² for the class data set. Walk through the first cell together on the board, then students complete independently. **Steps on board:** (1) Calculate expected values from total N and predicted ratio. (2) Fill in each column of the table. (3) Sum the final column = χ². (4) Determine degrees of freedom (number of categories − 1). (5) Compare χ² to the critical value at p = 0.05. (6) Write a conclusion sentence: *"Because our χ² of ___ is [less/greater] than the critical value of ___, we [fail to reject / reject] the null hypothesis that the data fit a ___ ratio."* **Prompt for struggling students:** *"Expected just means: if the ratio were perfect, how many of each type would you see out of [total]?"* |
| 1:17–1:27 | **Family letter (10 min)** | Students draft a short letter (scaffold provided) to the fictional family explaining: (1) the inheritance pattern of the trait, (2) the probability their next child will be affected, and (3) one sentence noting that this is a probability, not a guarantee, and what the chi-square test showed about real-world variation. **Scaffold prompts:** *"Dear [family name], Based on your family history, the trait appears to follow a ___ pattern. This means… The chance that your next child will be affected is approximately ___ because… It is important to know that this number is a probability, not a certainty…"* |
| 1:27–1:30 | **Collect & close** | Students staple pedigree analysis + chi-square template + family letter + student checklist. Submit. Closing cold-call: *"If your chi-square value was very large, what would that tell you?"* Preview Day 6. |

---

### Quick Chi-Square Write-Up Rubric (Teacher Use)

| Criterion | ✓+ (Strong) | ✓ (Adequate) | ✓− (Needs support) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Expected values** | Correctly calculated from total N and predicted ratio | Minor arithmetic error; method is sound | Method unclear or expected values not calculated |
| **χ² computation** | All columns correct; sum is accurate | 1 arithmetic error; final sum slightly off | Multiple errors or incomplete table |
| **Comparison to critical value** | Correct df; correct critical value identified; comparison statement accurate | Correct comparison but df not stated | Comparison missing or incorrect |
| **Conclusion sentence** | Uses "fail to reject / reject" language correctly; connects result to whether data support the Mendelian model | Conclusion present but uses informal language ("it worked") without connecting to the model | Conclusion missing or contradicts the numbers |

---

### Common Misconceptions to Watch For

Students often believe that if the chi-square test "fails" (i.e., they reject the null hypothesis), they did the experiment wrong, rather than understanding that the model itself may not fit or that sample size or procedure may need examination. They also frequently confuse "fail to reject the null" with "prove the null is true" — emphasize that the test only tells us the data are consistent with the model, not that the model is proven. During pedigree work, watch for students who assign carrier status to affected individuals (affected = homozygous recessive, not heterozygous) and students who assume that an unaffected individual in a recessive pedigree must be homozygous dominant when they could be a carrier. In the family letter, students sometimes state probabilities as certainties (*"Your child will be unaffected"*); redirect them to language of likelihood.

# Day 6: Summative Assessment — Family Inheritance Investigation (75 min)

### Learning Objectives (HS-LS3-1, HS-LS3-3; SEP: Using Mathematics, Analyzing & Interpreting Data, Obtaining/Evaluating/Communicating Information)
- Students will independently analyze a novel pedigree, assign genotypes, calculate offspring probabilities, evaluate class simulation data with a chi-square test, and communicate results in a family letter.

---

### Pedigree Selection
**Use an autosomal recessive pedigree.** This is the strongest choice because it requires students to reason about hidden carriers, which is the most common and most revealing point of confusion; autosomal dominant pedigrees are solvable by surface-level pattern matching and X-linked adds a variable (sex-linkage) that conflates two skills at once. Reserve X-linked for a future challenge problem or extension.

---

### Important Distinctions from Day 5
- **New family pedigree** (3 generations, 14 individuals — different names and structure than practice)
- **Individual work throughout** (no pairs)
- **Pre-collected class simulation data provided** (teacher runs coin-flip compilation from Day 5's data or generates a prepared data set so all students analyze the same numbers, eliminating simulation time and keeping the assessment within one period)

---

### Materials to Prepare
- Novel pedigree handout with starred individuals for genotype assignment (1 per student)
- Pre-compiled class offspring data table (printed on the handout or projected; ~400 flips, Bb × Bb cross, slight deviation from 3:1 to make chi-square meaningful)
- Chi-square calculation template (same format as Day 5)
- Critical value reference strip (printed on template)
- Family letter scaffold with sentence starters (for accommodated students; extras available)
- Codon chart not needed today
- Student checklist from Assessment 2 rubric packet (1 per student)

---

### Timed Sequence

| Time | Task | Student Produces |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:03 | Read instructions, review pedigree, ask clarifying questions (procedure only) | — |
| 0:03–0:20 | **Pedigree analysis:** Identify inheritance pattern with 2-sentence justification citing specific individuals; assign genotypes to all starred individuals; note and explain any uncertain genotypes | Annotated pedigree with written justification |
| 0:20–0:35 | **Probability calculation:** Construct a Punnett square for the specified cross; state probability of next child being affected as fraction and percent; write one interpretation sentence | Punnett square and probability statement |
| 0:35–0:50 | **Chi-square analysis:** Using the provided class data, calculate expected values, complete the chi-square table, compare to critical value, write a conclusion sentence about whether data support the predicted ratio | Completed chi-square template with conclusion |
| 0:50–0:70 | **Family letter:** Draft a short letter to the fictional family explaining the inheritance pattern, the probability, and why the prediction is a likelihood not a certainty; mention what the chi-square result reveals about real-world variation | Family letter (~150–200 words) |
| 0:70–0:75 | Self-check against printed student checklist, staple all pages, submit | Completed packet: pedigree + Punnett square + chi-square template + letter + checklist |

---

### Accommodations

| Need | Accommodation |
|---|---|
| **IEP / 504 — extended time** | Student completes pedigree analysis and Punnett square in class; finishes chi-square and family letter in resource period with sealed packet; deadline by end of school day |
| **IEP / 504 — reduced written output** | Accept bulleted family letter (must include same four content elements: pattern, probability, uncertainty language, chi-square connection); justification may be two bullet points instead of sentences |
| **ELL** | Family letter scaffold with sentence starters provided; key terms printed with parenthetical definitions on the pedigree handout (e.g., "carrier (a person who has one copy of the recessive allele but does not show the trait)"); extra time per IEP/504 if documented |
| **Physical / motor** | Allow typed responses; enlarge pedigree to 150% for visual accessibility |
| **Early finishers** | Flip the handout: printed extension prompt — *"If this family asked whether the trait could be X-linked instead of autosomal recessive, what specific evidence in the pedigree would you use to rule that out? Write 2–3 sentences."* |

---

### Realistic Scoring Plan (~25 students)

| Strategy | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Answer key prep (before class)** | Complete your own pedigree, Punnett square, chi-square, and letter in advance; mark acceptable genotype variations for uncertain individuals so grading decisions are instant |
| **First-pass sort (same day, ~15 min)** | Sort into three piles: (1) meets — pattern correct, genotypes consistent, chi-square complete, letter present; (2) borderline — one component weak; (3) follow-up — pattern wrong or multiple components missing |
| **Targeted scoring (planning period, ~35 min)** | Score the borderline pile criterion by criterion against the analytic rubric; spot-check the meets pile for chi-square conclusion accuracy (most common hidden error); score the follow-up pile fully and write one specific feedback comment per student |
| **Student checklist as filter** | Unchecked boxes flag exactly where students knew they were incomplete — check those sections first |
| **Return timeline** | Scores back by Day 8 (mid-Week 3) so students receive feedback before the policy brief |

---

### Teacher Set-Up & Grading Checklist (Printable)

> **Day 6 — Before Class**
> - [ ] Print novel pedigree handout with starred individuals and specified cross (1 per student)
> - [ ] Print or paste pre-compiled class simulation data onto handout (or confirm it is projected)
> - [ ] Print chi-square template with critical value strip (1 per student)
> - [ ] Print family letter scaffold with sentence starters (for accommodated students + extras)
> - [ ] Print student checklists (1 per student)
> - [ ] Prepare completed answer key with acceptable genotype variations noted
> - [ ] Confirm enlarged handouts printed for students who need them
> - [ ] Post timer or have projector timer ready
>
> **During Class**
> - [ ] Read instructions aloud; confirm individual work; clarify procedure questions only
> - [ ] Start visible timer at 0:03
> - [ ] Circulate silently — no content help; note students who are stuck for follow-up
> - [ ] Give transition cues at 0:20, 0:35, 0:50 (announce next section)
> - [ ] Give 5-minute warning at 0:65
> - [ ] Remind students to self-check and staple before submitting
> - [ ] Collect extended-time students' partial work and issue deadline passes
>
> **After Class**
> - [ ] First-pass sort into three piles: aim for same day
> - [ ] Detailed rubric scoring by end of Day 7
> - [ ] Record scores in gradebook
> - [ ] Write one targeted feedback comment per follow-up student
> - [ ] Note most common error for a 3-minute warm-up correction on Day 7 or 8
> - [ ] Return scored assessments by Day 8
